name: Operational maturity
explanation: Your team is new to running distributed systems, which these styles depend on (automation, monitoring, messaging).

name: Tiny beginner team
explanation: A team of 1–3 beginners would carry the whole operational load of many services.

name: No clear domains
explanation: The system doesn't split into clear business areas, so service boundaries would be guesswork.

name: Many teams and clear domains
explanation: Clear business areas plus many people make domain-partitioned styles a natural fit (one team per area).

name: Event workload
explanation: The system mainly reacts to events, which is what event-driven styles are built for.
otherwiseExplanation: You didn't say the system mainly reacts to events. For ordinary request-and-response work, asynchronous events add testing, debugging and consistency problems without paying them back.

name: Strict workflow
explanation: Workflows must be strictly controlled, which is hard with asynchronous, nondeterministic event flows.

name: Spiky concurrency
explanation: Very high, spiky concurrent load is the problem space-based architecture was designed for.
otherwiseExplanation: Space-based architecture's complexity only pays off under very high, spiky concurrent load, which you didn't select.

name: Sequential processing
explanation: Data flows through sequential steps, which is exactly what a pipeline does.
otherwiseExplanation: A pipeline only fits systems that process data in sequential steps, which you didn't select.

name: Plug-ins
explanation: You need plug-ins or per-customer customisation, which a microkernel is built for.
otherwiseExplanation: A microkernel's plug-in machinery only pays off when you need extensions or customisation, which you didn't select.

name: On-premise or single server
explanation: You must run on your own servers, so cloud-managed serverless isn't possible and heavily distributed styles get harder.

source.note: Serverless needs a cloud provider's managed runtime

name: VMs or containers only
explanation: You can only use VMs or containers, so provider-managed serverless functions aren't an option.

source.note: Serverless needs a cloud provider's managed runtime

name: Avoid lock-in
explanation: Serverless ties you to a provider's triggers, identity and services, which conflicts with avoiding lock-in.

name: Strict ACID transactions
explanation: You need all-or-nothing transactions across the system; styles built on async messaging or replicated data make that hard.

name: Legacy migration
explanation: You're moving away from a monolith; service-based architecture is a well-known stepping stone, and big-bang microservices rewrites are risky.

name: Steady heavy load
explanation: Constant heavy load is where pay-per-use serverless gets expensive compared with always-on servers.

name: Blast radius
explanation: Failures must only affect some customers, which is exactly what cells provide.
otherwiseExplanation: Cell-based architecture's cost and overhead only pay off when failures must be contained to a subset of customers, which you didn't select.

name: Regulated data
explanation: Regulated data needs strong security, so security counts at least High.

name: Peer-to-peer
explanation: Users or devices share directly, which is what peer-to-peer is for.
otherwiseExplanation: Peer-to-peer only fits when users or devices share directly without a central server, which you didn't select.

source.note: Niche style, gated by this characteristic

name: Edge processing
explanation: You need processing near devices or offline on site, which is what edge–cloud is for.
otherwiseExplanation: Edge–cloud only fits when you need on-site, low-latency or offline processing, which you didn't select.

name: New system, direction uncertain
explanation: Growth is stable or unknown and the system isn't planned to live 5+ years, so starting simple and evolving later is the safer bet.

name: Technical changes dominate
explanation: Most changes are technical (UI or database swaps); technical layers keep those changes in one place, while domain modules spread them everywhere.

name: Installed application
explanation: It runs only on each user's own computer or phone, so it ships as one deployable program. Styles that split a system into separately deployed services talking over a network don't fit. (Pick "On our server, plus an app people download" if you also run servers.)

source.locator: ch.9 and ch.19 (monolithic vs distributed: deployment units)

name: One set of quality needs
explanation: The whole system needs the same qualities, so one deployable unit (one architecture quantum) can serve it. Richards & Ford: a single set of characteristics means a monolith is suitable, even if other factors favour distribution.

name: Parts need different qualities
explanation: Parts of the system need different qualities, which points to several separately deployed units (quanta), i.e. a distributed style.

name: No clear need for microservices
explanation: Microservices pay off when several teams must release independently, or usage grows fast. Neither applies here, so their cost and running complexity aren't paid back. If parts of the system need different qualities, a few larger services (service-based) give that split more cheaply.

source.locator: ch.14, ch.18–19 (organisational factors; service-based as the pragmatic distributed style)

name: Parts with different needs
explanation: You said some parts of the system need very different qualities.

effects.message: Consider a hybrid: parts with different needs can be separate deployable units (architecture quanta), each with the style that suits it.

name: Several frontend teams
explanation: Several teams share one large web frontend.

effects.message: Consider micro-frontends as an add-on: each team owns and deploys its part of the web frontend.

name: Missing budget and team info
explanation: Budget, team size and experience are all "Not sure".

effects.message: Without budget or team info, results lean towards feature-rich distributed styles, which may underweight cost and complexity.

source.note: Warning when the inputs that balance cost and complexity are missing

name: Installed app plus back end
explanation: You're building an installed app and a back end you run.

effects.message: These are two separately deployed parts with different needs. The ranking mainly fits the back end. The installed app is one program on each device: usually a modular monolith, or a microkernel if it needs plug-ins.

name: Contradictory answers
explanation: You said it runs only on each user's device, and also that some parts need very different qualities.

effects.message: Two of your answers don't fit together. You said the software runs only on each user's own device, but parts with very different needs usually run as separate pieces on servers. If people use it in a browser, or through an app that talks to your server, change "Where will your software run?" to one of the server answers. As it stands, the ranking treats it as one installed program.
